analogy.p: Think of a river as a bath. Rain is the tap running: the heavier the rain, the faster the bath fills. The channel is the bath itself, and flooding is water spilling over the edge when more arrives than the plug can drain. Urbanisation is like putting a funnel on the tap and a bigger waste pipe on the ground floor: the water gets there much faster. Hard engineering is like raising the sides of the bath (embankments) or adding an overflow pipe (relief channel); soft engineering is like turning the tap down (trees) or keeping your valuables on the top shelf (zoning and warnings). The analogy breaks down because a river is not a closed tub: what you do upstream changes what happens downstream, and the bath has no neighbours to flood.
analogy.t: A river is a bath with the plug and the taps

bullets: Know the **physical causes** of flooding: prolonged and heavy rainfall, geology, relief, saturated ground and snowmelt.
Know the **human causes**: urbanisation (impermeable surfaces and drains), deforestation, and some farming practices.
Be able to draw, label and interpret a **hydrograph**: rainfall, discharge, base flow, rising limb, peak discharge, falling limb, lag time.
Know hard engineering: **dams and reservoirs, straightening, embankments, flood relief channels**.
Know soft engineering: **flood warnings and preparation, flood plain zoning, planting trees, river restoration**.
Know a **UK case study** (for example the Jubilee River scheme at Maidenhead, Windsor and Eton, but check your own class example) with reasons, issues and effects.
Command words: **describe**, **explain**, **suggest**, **assess**, **evaluate**, **to what extent**.
**Link to other topics:** river processes and landforms (floodplains and levees), weather and climate change, and the UK coast (the same hard/soft idea).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: For flood risk and management, AQA expects you to explain the **physical and human causes of flooding**, interpret **hydrographs**, and describe and evaluate **hard engineering** and **soft engineering** strategies for reducing the risk. You then apply all of this to a **case study of a flood management scheme in the UK**, showing why the scheme was needed and the social, economic and environmental issues it caused or solved. This topic is a favourite for the 6-mark and 9-mark extended answers because it asks you to weigh up advantages and disadvantages, so you should practise writing balanced evaluations that end with a judgement.

bullets: Flood = discharge exceeds channel capacity, so water **overflows the banks**.
**Flood risk** = chance of a flood x its likely impact on people, property and the environment.
Water reaches the river by **surface runoff** (fast), **throughflow** (moderate) and **groundwater flow** (slow).
Fast routes to the channel give **high peak discharge** and short lag time (a flashy river).
Slower routes give lower, later peaks (a gentle river).
**Infiltration** is water soaking into the soil; **interception** is water caught by leaves and branches.
Rivers flood naturally, and floods deposit **fertile alluvium** on floodplains: not all flooding is harmful.
Exam tip: to explain a cause, show how it makes water reach the river **faster or in greater volume**.
core.h: Flood basics: what is a flood and why does the risk vary?
core.p: A river **floods** when its discharge becomes greater than the capacity of the channel, so water spills over the banks onto the floodplain. The **flood risk** of a place is the chance of flooding combined with the damage it would cause, and it depends on both physical features of the drainage basin and human activity within it. The key idea is that a flood happens when water reaches the river **faster** than the river can carry it away, so anything that increases **surface runoff** (water flowing over the surface) or speeds up the journey of water to the channel increases flood risk. Anything that slows the water down, such as trees, soil and gentle slopes, decreases it.

bullets: **Heavy, prolonged rainfall:** more water than the ground can absorb; intense storms cause **flash floods**.
**Saturated soil** (from previous rain): no more infiltration, so extra rain becomes **surface runoff**.
**Impermeable rock** (clay, granite): little infiltration, high runoff, high drainage density (many streams).
**Steep relief:** water flows downhill quickly, reaching the channel fast, reducing lag time.
**Snowmelt** and **frozen ground:** sudden release of water that cannot soak in.
**Round-shaped drainage basin:** tributaries all deliver water at about the same time, giving a **high, sharp peak**.
**Lack of vegetation** (bare ground or moorland) means less interception and less water taken up by plants.
**Link to other topics:** UK weather (low pressure systems) and climate change increase the frequency of heavy rain.
core.p: The physical causes are natural features of the weather, rocks and landscape. **Prolonged or intense rainfall** delivers more water than the soil can absorb, and if it follows a wet period the ground is already **saturated**, so almost all the new rain runs straight off the surface. **Impermeable geology** such as clay or granite does not let water soak in, so it runs off quickly, whereas permeable rock such as chalk absorbs it. **Steep slopes** make water run into the river faster, and **snowmelt** in spring releases a large volume of water in a short time, especially if the ground is frozen so the water cannot infiltrate. The shape of the drainage basin also matters: a round basin sends water to the same point at the same time, which raises the peak discharge.

bullets: **Urbanisation:** impermeable surfaces (roads, roofs) and **drains** cause rapid surface runoff.
**Deforestation:** less interception, less transpiration, more runoff and more soil erosion filling the channel.
**Farming:** compacted or bare soil, ploughing up and down slopes, field drains: all speed up runoff.
**Building on floodplains** increases the number of people and buildings at risk.
**Climate change** is raising sea levels and making intense rainfall more frequent (a human cause on a global scale).
Sediment from soil erosion can raise the river bed, reducing channel capacity.
Urban rivers are **flashy** because water is delivered quickly in huge volume.
Exam tip: always say what the human activity does to **infiltration and runoff**, then to the **speed and volume** of water reaching the river.
core.p: People increase flood risk mainly by changing the surface of the land. **Urbanisation** replaces soil and plants with tarmac, concrete and roofs, which are impermeable, so rain cannot infiltrate and runs directly into **drains and sewers** that discharge into the river quickly. **Deforestation** removes trees, which means less interception and less water taken up by roots and transpired, so more water reaches the river faster. Some farming practices, such as ploughing downhill, leaving bare soil in winter, compacting soil with heavy machinery and draining fields, also increase runoff. Building on the floodplain does not make flooding more likely but it greatly increases the **damage** caused when it happens, and climate change is making heavy rainfall more frequent.

bullets: **Rainfall:** shown as bars at the top (or side) of the graph.
**Base flow:** the normal, steady discharge fed by groundwater when it has not rained.
**Rising limb:** the part of the line where discharge increases as runoff reaches the river.
**Peak discharge:** the maximum discharge reached, in cumecs (cubic metres per second).
**Falling limb:** the part of the line where discharge decreases after the peak.
**Lag time:** the time between **peak rainfall** and **peak discharge**.
**Steep rising limb, high peak and short lag time** = flashy river with high flood risk.
**Gentle rising limb, lower peak and long lag time** = lower flood risk.
core.p: A storm hydrograph is a graph showing how a river's **discharge** changes over time in response to a period of rainfall. Rainfall is shown as bars and discharge as a line. Before the storm the discharge is steady at the **base flow**, water that reaches the river slowly via groundwater. After the rain, discharge rises along the **rising limb** to reach the **peak discharge**, the highest discharge, and then drops along the **falling limb** back to base flow. The **lag time** is the time between the peak rainfall and the peak discharge, and it tells you how quickly water reaches the river: a short lag time means a flashy river and high flood risk.

bullets: Quote **values with units**: for example 'peak discharge of 60 cumecs at 8 hours'.
Calculate **lag time** = time of peak discharge - time of peak rainfall.
Calculate **increase in discharge** = peak discharge - base flow.
**Urban:** impermeable surfaces and drains, so rapid runoff, high peak, short lag time.
**Rural/forested:** infiltration and interception, so slow flow, lower peak, long lag time.
**Steep, impermeable catchments** are flashy; **flat, permeable** catchments are gentle.
After storms the **ground may be saturated**, so a second storm gives a higher, faster peak.
Exam tip: when asked to 'explain the difference', link each difference in the graph to one cause.
core.h: Using hydrographs to compare rivers and causes
core.p: Examiners often give two hydrographs and ask you to compare them or explain the difference. Always compare using **data**: quote the peak discharge and the lag time for each, with units, and do a calculation if asked. Then use the physical and human causes to explain why one is flashier. An urban catchment with impermeable surfaces and drains will have a short lag time and a high peak, whereas a rural, wooded or permeable-rock catchment will have a longer lag time and a lower peak, because water takes longer to reach the channel. The gradient of the rising limb is the quickest visual clue: steeper means water arrives faster.

bullets: **Dams and reservoirs:** reduce flood peaks, provide water, power and recreation; but very **expensive**, drown farmland and homes, trap sediment and harm wildlife.
**Straightening:** quickly removes water from a place, protects the town; but **increases flood risk downstream**, destroys habitats and can cause bank erosion.
Both **reduce lag time or flow** but do not stop flooding in a very large storm.
Hard engineering usually **protects a specific place** very well.
High **upfront and maintenance costs**: often only affordable for protecting large towns.
Often unattractive and **change the natural look** of the river.
Hard engineering can give people a **false sense of security** so they build on the floodplain.
**Link to other topics:** the same structures (sea walls, groynes) are used on the coast.
core.h: Hard engineering: dams and reservoirs, straightening
core.p: **Hard engineering** means using artificial structures to control the river and protect people from flooding. A **dam and reservoir** holds back water in a valley in times of heavy rain and releases it slowly, which reduces peak discharge downstream and also provides water supply and hydroelectric power and recreation. Channel **straightening** replaces a meandering section with a straight, often lined, channel so that water travels through faster and flood water is removed quickly from a town. Both can be effective but they are expensive, change the natural environment and can cause problems elsewhere: for example, a straightened river sends water downstream faster, which can **increase flood risk further downstream**.

bullets: **Embankments:** raise the river banks; **cheap and effective** for small floods; but can **burst**, look ugly and can push the flood problem downstream.
Embankments **cut the river off from its floodplain**, preventing natural flooding and reducing deposition of fertile alluvium.
**Flood relief channels:** divert water around a town, very effective and reliable.
Relief channels are **expensive**, use up **farmland** and can disturb wildlife during building.
Relief channels may **not work** if designed for smaller floods than occur.
Embankments and relief channels often need **regular maintenance** and checking.
In evaluating, compare **cost, effectiveness, environmental impact and long-term sustainability**.
Exam tip: always give both an **advantage and a disadvantage** for each method in an evaluation.
core.h: Hard engineering: embankments and flood relief channels
core.p: **Embankments** are raised banks built along the river (often from earth, concrete or stone) which increase the capacity of the channel so that it can hold more water before flooding. A **flood relief channel** is an artificial channel that takes water around a town: when the river reaches a certain level, some of the water is diverted into the relief channel and bypasses the vulnerable area before rejoining the river downstream. Embankments are cheap compared with dams but can fail if overtopped, and they can cut the river off from its floodplain; relief channels protect large urban areas very effectively but cost a lot, take up farmland and habitats, and need maintenance.

bullets: **Flood warnings and preparation:** cheap, saves lives and reduces damage; but needs **people to respond** and gives no protection to buildings.
**Flood plain zoning:** low cost, long-term, prevents damage to valuable property; but **cannot help existing built-up areas** and can restrict development.
**Planting trees:** increases **interception and infiltration**, stabilises soil and creates habitat; but takes **years to work** and needs land.
**River restoration:** removes artificial channels and embankments, re-creates **meanders and wetlands**; but needs space and may flood farmland.
Soft engineering is **sustainable**, cheaper and better for **wildlife and landscape**.
It is generally **less effective** than hard engineering in protecting existing towns from big floods.
It often needs **people's co-operation** and long planning.
Exam tip: link each method to what it does to **runoff, storage or exposure** (how many people are at risk).
core.h: Soft engineering: warnings, preparation, zoning, planting trees, river restoration
core.p: **Soft engineering** works with the natural river system rather than against it, and is generally cheaper and more sustainable than hard engineering. **Flood warnings and preparation** (such as the Environment Agency's flood alert system, flood plans and sandbags) give people time to move belongings and evacuate, which reduces damage and risk to life but does not stop the flood itself. **Flood plain zoning** controls land use so that open spaces like parks and playing fields are on the land closest to the river, while homes, schools and hospitals are located in safer areas. **Planting trees** in the river's catchment increases interception and transpiration and slows runoff, and **river restoration** returns a river to a more natural state (for example by removing embankments or re-creating meanders) so water can spread on to the floodplain and is stored there.

bullets: Use **criteria**: cost, effectiveness, sustainability, environmental impact, social impact.
Say **for whom** it is good or bad: residents, farmers, people downstream, wildlife.
Use **comparative words**: 'more expensive than', 'less effective than', 'whereas'.
A 9-mark answer should include **a conclusion** that is a clear judgement (e.g. 'a mixture is best because ...').
Large towns with valuable property justify **expensive hard engineering**; rural areas often use **soft engineering**.
Remember strategies can **interact**: trees upstream reduce the size of the flood the embankments must hold.
Link to the **case study** with named facts to support your points.
**Link to other topics:** the same evaluation structure applies to coastal management.
core.h: Hard versus soft engineering: how to evaluate
core.p: To **evaluate** strategies you must weigh advantages against disadvantages and then reach a justified judgement, rather than just listing facts. Think about **cost** (initial and maintenance), **effectiveness** (how much it reduces flooding and for how long), **sustainability** (can it continue without harming the future), **environmental impact** (habitats and landscape) and **who benefits** (the whole community or just one area). Hard engineering usually protects places very effectively and quickly but is expensive and damaging to the environment, whereas soft engineering is cheaper and more sustainable but less effective in large floods. A top-mark answer often concludes that a **combination** of strategies, matched to the size and value of the area at risk, is best.

bullets: **Why it was needed:** the towns lie on the **floodplain** of the Thames, with many homes and businesses at risk, and a history of damaging floods (including 1947).
**What was built:** the **Jubilee River** flood relief channel (hard engineering) plus works on the main river, with **weirs and gates** controlling how much water is diverted.
**Social:** protects thousands of homes, reducing risk, stress and insurance problems; the channel also creates public footpaths and recreation.
**Economic:** costs of building were very high (of the order of £100 million), but it avoids huge flood damage costs for homes and businesses.
**Environmental:** created new **wildlife habitats** along the channel, but building it **took up farmland and changed the landscape**.
**Problems:** the scheme has needed repairs and maintenance, and floods in winter 2013-14 showed that it cannot remove all risk in extreme floods.
Possible negative: some people **downstream** may be at greater risk because more water leaves the protected area faster.
Exam tip: in a case-study question include **at least three specific facts** (place names, dates, structures, costs) not just general points, and check these against your own notes.
core.h: UK case study: a flood management scheme (Jubilee River, Maidenhead, Windsor and Eton)
core.p: The Maidenhead, Windsor and Eton Flood Alleviation Scheme on the River Thames in Berkshire was built because these towns have a **history of flooding**, with large areas of homes and businesses on the Thames floodplain at risk, and serious floods in 1947 caused particular damage. The main part of the scheme is the **Jubilee River**, an artificial **flood relief channel** around 11 km long which opened in 2002 and takes excess water around the three towns, together with **improvements to the existing river channels**. The scheme cost of the order of £100 million, and protects thousands of properties. Your class may have studied a different scheme such as the Somerset Levels or Cumbria; use the structure below and replace the details with your own named facts.

bullets: **Location:** name the river, the towns and the county or region.
**Reasons:** flood history (dates and damage), number of properties at risk, and physical/human causes.
**Strategies:** name each hard and soft method used, and what each does.
**Social effects:** safety, homes protected, stress, insurance, recreation.
**Economic effects:** cost of the scheme, value of damage prevented, effects on businesses and farmland.
**Environmental effects:** habitats created or lost, landscape changes, effect on river processes.
**Evaluation:** was it a success, what are its limits, and who gained or lost?
Practice writing a **9-mark** answer from this checklist in 12 minutes with specific facts.
core.h: Case-study answer structure: how to write about any scheme
core.p: Whatever scheme you studied, you can organise your case study using a short checklist so that nothing is missed in an exam. Begin with **location and context** (river, town, how often it floods), then the **reasons the scheme was needed** (past flood events, risk to property and people), the **strategies used** (hard and soft), and the **social, economic and environmental effects**, both positive and negative. End with an overall evaluation of how successful it has been and any lessons learned. Examiners reward specific, named detail, so learn a few facts perfectly rather than many vaguely.

exam: **Describe a hydrograph:** name the base flow, rising limb, peak discharge with value and time, falling limb, and calculate the lag time.
**Compare two hydrographs:** use data for both, one comparison per mark, with comparative words such as 'higher' and 'shorter'.
**Explain a cause of flooding (2 to 4 marks):** state the factor, then link to infiltration or runoff, then to speed or volume of water reaching the river.
**Use the correct command word:** describe = what; explain = why (because, so); evaluate = weigh up and give a judgement.
**Name a method and a reason:** 'embankments raise the banks, increasing capacity of the channel' earns two marks.
**For 6 marks:** give two strategies, each with an advantage and a disadvantage, and a final judgement.

**For 9 marks (extended):** use a clear structure, compare strategies using criteria (cost, effectiveness, environmental impact), use named facts from your case study, and finish with a justified conclusion.
**Calculations:** lag time = peak discharge time - peak rainfall time; increase in discharge = peak - base flow; show working and units.
**Case study questions:** include place names, dates, costs and structures; split your answer into social, economic and environmental.
**SPaG-style tip:** use paragraphs and connectives such as 'however', 'whereas', 'as a result' to link your argument.

mistakes.r: Lag time is the time between **peak rainfall** and **peak discharge**.
mistakes.w: Lag time is the time it takes for the river to flood.

mistakes.r: Urban areas flood because **impermeable surfaces and drains** cause rapid runoff, not because of more rain.
mistakes.w: Urban areas flood because it rains more in cities.

mistakes.r: Trees **reduce** runoff through interception and transpiration, but do not stop floods in extreme storms.
It is effective but **expensive, harms the environment** and may shift flooding downstream; evaluation needs both sides.
mistakes.w: Hard engineering is always best because it is the strongest.

mistakes.r: Soft engineering reduces the **risk or the damage** and is cheaper and more sustainable; it is just less effective for big floods.
mistakes.w: Soft engineering does nothing to stop floods.

mistakes.r: It removes water faster from one place but can **increase flood risk downstream**.
mistakes.w: Straightening the river reduces flooding everywhere.

mistakes.r: Use **data with units**, such as peak discharge in cumecs and lag time in hours.
It does not stop floods; it **reduces damage** by keeping valuable buildings out of high-risk areas.
mistakes.w: Flood plain zoning stops floods happening.

mistakes.r: Use **named facts** (place, date, structure, cost) from your own case study.
mistakes.w: Case study answers that are general.

summary: You must be able to explain the physical and human causes of river flooding, interpret storm hydrographs, describe and evaluate hard engineering (dams and reservoirs, straightening, embankments, flood relief channels) and soft engineering (warnings and preparation, flood plain zoning, planting trees, river restoration), and apply these to a UK flood management case study. It matters because evaluation of flood management is a regular high-mark question in Paper 1.

terms.d: When the discharge of a river exceeds the capacity of its channel and water flows onto the floodplain.
The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries.
Water that flows over the surface of the land into a river.
The process of water soaking into the soil from the surface.
Rainfall caught and held by leaves, branches and other vegetation before it reaches the ground.
Not allowing water to pass through, so water runs off the surface.
A graph showing how the discharge of a river changes over time in response to rainfall.
The volume of water passing a point in a river each second, measured in cumecs (m3/s).
The normal, steady flow in a river, fed by groundwater.
The part of a hydrograph where discharge increases after rainfall.
The highest discharge reached on a hydrograph.
The part of a hydrograph where discharge decreases after the peak.
The time between the peak rainfall and the peak discharge.
Using artificial structures to control rivers and protect against flooding.
Managing flood risk in a more sustainable way by working with natural processes.
An artificial channel that takes flood water around a vulnerable area.
Planning land use according to flood risk, so that valuable buildings are kept away from areas most likely to flood.
Returning a river to a more natural state, for example by removing embankments and re-creating meanders.

worked.ans: Rural lag time = 5 hours; urban lag time = 2 hours (2 marks). The urban river has a much higher peak discharge (60 cumecs compared with 25 cumecs) and a shorter lag time (3 hours less), so it is flashier with a higher flood risk (2 marks).
worked.q: Table: Rural river hydrograph: peak rainfall at 2 hours, peak discharge of 25 cumecs at 7 hours, base flow 5 cumecs. Urban river: peak rainfall at 2 hours, peak discharge of 60 cumecs at 4 hours, base flow 5 cumecs. Calculate the lag time for each and compare the two rivers. (4 marks)
steps: Rural increase in discharge = 25 - 5 = 20 cumecs; urban = 60 - 5 = 55 cumecs.
Compare: urban lag time is 3 hours shorter and its peak is 35 cumecs higher (60 - 25).

worked.ans: Urban areas have impermeable surfaces such as tarmac, concrete and roofs, so water cannot infiltrate into the soil (1). The water runs off as surface runoff into drains and sewers (1), which carry it quickly into the river (1). This means the lag time is shorter and the peak discharge is higher, so the river is more likely to overflow its banks (1). (4 marks)
worked.q: Explain why urbanisation increases flood risk. (4 marks)
steps: Drains and sewers carry water quickly.
Surface runoff reaches the river faster.
Result: shorter lag time, higher peak discharge.

worked.ans: Hard engineering such as embankments and flood relief channels can be very effective at protecting towns. Embankments raise the banks and so increase the channel's capacity, and they are cheaper than many other hard methods, but they can burst if overtopped and can increase flood risk downstream. A flood relief channel diverts water around a town, protecting thousands of properties, but it is very expensive to build, uses up farmland and changes the natural landscape. Hard engineering also gives a false sense of security, so more people may build on the floodplain. In contrast, soft engineering such as flood warnings and zoning is cheaper and more sustainable but gives less protection against large floods. Overall, hard engineering is justified in large, valuable urban areas where the benefits outweigh the costs, but a combination with soft engineering is probably best. (6 marks)
worked.q: Evaluate the use of hard engineering to reduce the risk of flooding. (6 marks)
steps: Name two methods, e.g. embankments and a flood relief channel.
One advantage and one disadvantage for each.
Give a judgement with a reason.
